Alex / team —

Great — we'll take the 10:00 PT slot, sending calendar invite. Below are the practical implementation notes I promised:

1) SDK quickstart (Node + Python examples) — keep client libs pinned to our minor-stable channel for GA models. Example Node usage:

// Node sample (retry/backoff recommended)
const Redwood = require('@redwood/inference');
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_TEST_KEY, baseUrl: 'https://api.redwood.ai/v2' });

async function generate(prompt) {
  return await client.text.generate({
    model: 'redwood-3-small',
    prompt,
    maxTokens: 256
  });
}

2) Retry & timeout strategy (recommended):
- Client-side timeouts: 10s for short inference calls, 30s for longer streaming/generation.
- Retries: use idempotent-safe retries for non-streaming requests only.
- Backoff: exponential backoff with jitter (initial 200ms, factor 2, max 4s, cap 3 retries) for 429/503.
- For 5xx or network errors, allow up to 2 additional retries with linear backoff and logging.

Edge handling for bursts:
- If you see repeated 429s at scale, add a token-bucket local rate limiter to smooth spikes and fall back to degrade gracefully (reduce requests to lower-cost model variant).

3) Endpoint migration (v1 -> v2 zero-downtime):
- Dual-write traffic: route 5-10% of traffic to v2 via header flag for 48 hours and monitor latency/quality.
- Canary headers: X-Redwood-Canary: launchpad-v2.
- Fallback: automatic routing policy will revert to v1 if p50 latency increases by >25% or error rate >2%.

4) Instrumentation & observability: include request_id from our SDK in logs, capture model, token counts, and latency per call. We'll provide a dashboard template in the Drive link.

I'll also attach a minimal patch (redwood_sdk_quickstart.patch) with code examples and a sample health-check script your infra can run.

Marissa Cole

Thanks — two clarifications from our side:

- Bursts: During campaign spikes we may send short-lived bursts of 200 qps for <10s windows. Is the token-bucket approach sufficient or do you recommend an upstream queue?
- Billing/rate limits: What's the per-minute token limit on Hosted tier and what's the recommended approach if we want predictable throughput (reserved capacity)?

If reserved capacity is the right path we want a ballpark cost for a committed 50 qps pool vs the hosted usage.

—Priya

Subject: Re: LaunchPad integration: SDK onboarding + retry & rate-limit guidance

Priya / Alex —

Short answers:

- For very short, high bursts (200 qps < 10s), a client-side token-bucket combined with a small upstream queue (edge buffer) is the most reliable pattern. The token-bucket smooths short spikes; the edge buffer prevents transient overload while preserving request ordering for critical flows. We'll help you validate queue sizing during the integration tests.

- Hosted tier rate limits: default soft limit 18,000 tokens/minute per project (subject to model and token size). That's typically sufficient for moderate bursty traffic but not 200 qps sustained spikes.

- Reserved capacity: recommended if you want predictable throughput. Ballpark: committed 50 qps pool on our Dedicated offering starts at $X,XXX/month (I'll have Sales provide a formal quote post-kickoff). Reserved capacity gives you guaranteed concurrency, custom autoscaling policies, and lower per-token unit cost.

Next operational steps for the kickoff:
1) Confirm calendar invite for Thu 8/13 10:00 PT (sent).
2) Alex to share test keys and a small sample payload that represents a worst-case prompt.
3) We'll run a staged load test in our staging region and tune token-bucket + queue settings; deliver recommendations in the post-kickoff runbook.
